title: The Postcards of the fourth floor walk-up
premise: Theo Sterling, a ghostwriter of other people's letters, has spent six years mailing postcards to 4B Marigold Court — the walk-up where they grew up with their grandmother, and which burned down with every unsaid word still inside it. When the charred lot is auctioned to developers, Theo returns to the neighborhood they abandoned, confronting Odile, the foster sister who stayed behind, and Mr. Anselm, the retired postman who never delivered a single one of those postcards because he couldn't bear to. As demolition day approaches, Theo must finally write the letter they've been circling for years — to their grandmother's memory, to Odile, to themselves — and read it aloud in the empty stairwell before the walls come down.
about_author: Felix Oyelaran is the pen name of a former postal clerk who spent a decade sorting undeliverable mail in a mid-sized city, where he began collecting the stories of letters that arrived too late. He writes quietly devastating fiction about the small architectures of grief and lives near a river he refuses to name.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. In their cramped apartment, Theo catalogs postcards written but never received — one per week for six years, all addressed to 4B Marigold Court. We learn they write other people's love letters for a living while their own words go nowhere. Emotional beat: tender, controlled loneliness; the ritual that keeps grief at arm's length.

chapters.title: Return to Sender
chapters.summary: Mr. Anselm's POV. The retired postman sorts through a shoebox of undelivered postcards at his kitchen table, unable to throw them away or deliver them. A flashback shows the morning after the fire, when he made his choice. Emotional beat: quiet complicity; guilt worn like an old uniform.

chapters.title: Notice of Sale
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. A legal notice arrives: the lot at Marigold Court enters probate auction. Theo's hands shake over breakfast; their employer notices a typo in a client's condolence letter. Emotional beat: shock cracking open routine; the past acquiring a deadline.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Across town, Odile runs a small tailoring shop three blocks from the burned lot, sewing buttons onto coats she'll never wear herself. She sees the auction notice taped to a lamppost. Emotional beat: wary anticipation; she knew this day would come.

chapters.title: Marigold Court, Present Tense
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo takes the bus back to the old neighborhood for the first time in years, walking the block, cataloging what survived: the bodega, the crooked lamppost, the fence around the ruin. Emotional beat: disorientation; memory overlaying a changed street.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile remembers the night of the fire — how she pulled Theo out, how Grandma Ruth went back for the photo album and didn't come out, how Theo left within the month and never called. Emotional beat: buried anger surfacing; love braided with resentment.

chapters.title: Anselm's Route
chapters.summary: Mr. Anselm's POV. Anselm walks his old mail route on instinct, passing the lot, and spots Theo standing at the fence. Neither speaks. Emotional beat: recognition across distance; two keepers of the same secret seeing each other.

chapters.title: The Auction House
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. At the preview, Theo finds Lot 47: a water-damaged steamer trunk recovered from the stairwell, contents unexamined. They register to bid without deciding to. Emotional beat: compulsion; grief finding a purchase price.

chapters.title: Fitting Sessions
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile alters a suit for the developer's lawyer and hears about the trunk — and about a pale bidder who registered under the name Sterling. Emotional beat: alarm sharpening into resolve; she won't let Theo face this alone, even if she says otherwise.

chapters.title: Lot 47
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The auction. Theo bids against a reseller and wins the trunk with money meant for rent. Inside: Grandma Ruth's photo album, water-swollen but legible, and a bundle of letters addressed to Theo in her handwriting, never sent. Emotional beat: vertigo; the dead speaking back.

chapters.title: Letters I Never Opened
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, late night. Theo reads the first of Ruth's unsent letters — dated months before the fire, asking why Theo had gone so quiet. They can't finish it. Emotional beat: shame and tenderness colliding; the inventory of unsaid things growing heavier.

chapters.title: Three Blocks
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile closes the shop early and walks to Theo's building, standing outside for forty minutes before knocking. When Theo opens the door, neither apologizes first. Emotional beat: brittle reunion; old wounds wearing new politeness.

chapters.title: Coffee, No Sugar
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Theo and Odile drink coffee at a diner and trade careful updates — jobs, health, anything but the fire, the letters, the years between. Emotional beat: surface conversation hiding undertow; both testing whether the bridge holds weight.

chapters.title: The Postman Confesses
chapters.summary: Mr. Anselm's POV. Anselm visits Odile's shop to have a coat mended and, instead, confesses: he kept every postcard Theo ever mailed to 4B. He gives them to her. Emotional beat: relief and dread; a secret changing hands.

chapters.title: Six Years of Weather
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile reads the postcards at her counter after closing — six years of small reports, jokes, non-sequiturs, each one a message in a bottle thrown at a burned wall. She cries once, briefly, then locks them in the register drawer. Emotional beat: heartbreak disguised as bookkeeping.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Fence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Odile confronts Theo at the lot: 'You wrote to a building. You couldn't write to me.' Theo admits they didn't know how to be forgiven. Emotional beat: the fight they owed each other for six years, finally had.

chapters.title: Demolition Permit
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo learns the demolition date — three weeks out — and that the developer will raze the neighboring buildings' shared stairwell wall, the last physical piece of 4B. Emotional beat: countdown pressure; time becoming an antagonist.

chapters.title: Ruth's Second Letter
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo finishes Ruth's second unsent letter, which reveals she knew Theo was struggling and wrote anyway, weekly, hoping words would outlast silence. Emotional beat: being seen by the dead; grief softening into inheritance.

chapters.title: The Tailor's Measure
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile measures Theo for a new coat — their first physical closeness since childhood — and remembers teaching them to sew a button at this same table's predecessor. Emotional beat: repair in miniature; hands remembering what mouths forgot.

chapters.title: Neighbors
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, brief vignettes. The block reacts to the coming demolition: the bodega owner, the kids who use the lot as a shortcut, Mrs. Ferreira who waters a tree planted by Ruth. Emotional beat: a neighborhood as chorus; belonging larger than one family.

chapters.title: Anselm's Last Delivery
chapters.summary: Mr. Anselm's POV. Anselm asks Odile to return the postcards to Theo properly — delivered at last, by hand, with apology. She refuses; some deliveries aren't his to make anymore. Emotional beat: letting go of penance; forgiveness isn't transactional.

chapters.title: The Trunk's False Bottom
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Cleaning the trunk, Theo finds a false bottom containing Ruth's deed, a savings passbook in Theo's name, and a note: 'For the fourth floor, whoever climbs it.' Emotional beat: stunned generosity; a legacy with instructions implied but not given.

chapters.title: What Theo Almost Said
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo drafts the real letter — to Ruth, to Odile, to themselves — and burns the draft in a sink, panicking. Emotional beat: self-sabotage at the threshold; the oldest fear: that saying it aloud makes it final.

chapters.title: Odile's Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile balances her shop's books and realizes she's been keeping a second ledger — every kindness Theo failed to return, tallied for years. She closes it, deliberately, and doesn't balance the column. Emotional beat: choosing release over arithmetic.

chapters.title: Rain on Marigold Court
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A storm floods the lot; Theo and Odile, sheltering in the bodega doorway, end up laughing for the first time together in six years. Emotional beat: weather as grace; laughter as the first honest language between them.

chapters.title: The Developer's Offer
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The developer offers Theo money for the trunk's story — 'local color' for marketing the new building. Theo nearly signs. Emotional beat: temptation to monetize grief; the easy exit that would betray everything.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile organizes the neighbors to request the stairwell wall be preserved in the new build — a long shot petition. Theo watches her fight for a building that hurt them both. Emotional beat: reluctant admiration; watching someone love what you fled.

chapters.title: Ruth's Third Letter
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The third letter contains Ruth's account of the fire's eve — an ordinary evening, beans on the stove, Theo's chair empty again — and ends: 'Say it out loud, child. Walls don't need it. You do.' Emotional beat: instruction from beyond; the thesis arriving.

chapters.title: Two Weeks
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. With demolition imminent, Theo and Odile work side by side salvaging bricks from the fence line, barely speaking, entirely communicating. Emotional beat: companionship rebuilt through labor; silence turned useful.

chapters.title: Anselm's Box, Returned
chapters.summary: Mr. Anselm's POV. Theo visits Anselm, not to accuse but to thank him — for keeping the postcards safe, even wrongly. Anselm weeps into his tea. Emotional beat: mercy toward the flawed; the postman finally off duty.

chapters.title: The Petition Fails
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The city denies the preservation request. Odile takes it hard; Theo finds her in the dark shop and, for the first time, comforts instead of fleeing. Emotional beat: role reversal; the leaver learning to stay.

chapters.title: Draft After Draft
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo writes and discards eleven versions of the goodbye letter, then stops writing altogether and sits with the blank page. Emotional beat: the crisis of the writer who cannot write the true thing; surrender as beginning.

chapters.title: Odile's Confession
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile admits she almost sold the shop and left too, years ago — she stayed out of spite as much as loyalty, and resented Theo for escaping a trap she built herself. Emotional beat: the caretaker's hidden cost; truth as gift.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Eve of demolition. Theo, Odile, and Anselm share a meal in the shuttered bodega, lit by camping lanterns, telling Ruth stories. Emotional beat: vigil; found family assembling itself around a table that isn't there yet.

chapters.title: The Stairwell
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Dawn. Theo climbs the surviving exterior stairs of the adjacent building to the bricked outline of 4B's door, letter in hand. Emotional beat: ascent; every step a year.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo reads the letter aloud in the open air — to Ruth, to Odile below, to the block — every unsaid thing said at last, voice breaking and continuing. Odile answers from the ground: 'We heard you.' Emotional beat: climax; catharsis earned, not granted.

chapters.title: Walls Coming Down
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The demolition proceeds; neighbors watch from the sidewalk. Theo holds Odile's hand. Anselm salutes. The dust rises like weather. Emotional beat: witnessed ending; destruction as ceremony rather than erasure.

chapters.title: The Passbook
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo withdraws Ruth's savings and puts a deposit on a third-floor apartment two blocks from Odile's shop — not the fourth floor, not yet, but climbable. Emotional beat: hope with modest dimensions; belonging chosen, not inherited.

chapters.title: First Postcard, New Address
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile finds a postcard in her shop's mail slot: Theo's handwriting, addressed to her, current address, one line — 'Saving you a seat on the stairs.' Emotional beat: the ritual transformed; mail that arrives.

chapters.title: Everything Said
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, coda. One year later: Sunday dinner at Odile's, Anselm visiting with his box finally empty, Theo writing letters for strangers that now end well. On the windowsill, the photo album, restored. Emotional beat: resolution; memory kept not by preserving walls but by continuing the conversation.
